title: Middle Ear in Paediatrics
subject: Paediatrics
summary: The middle ear is a small air‑filled cavity behind the tympanic membrane, connected to the nasopharynx by the Eustachian tube. In children it is prone to infection, effusion and perforation, especially in low‑resource settings where viral URIs, malnutrition and lack of vaccination are common.

sections.p: The middle ear is the cavity between the tympanic membrane and the inner ear, lined by mucosa and containing the ossicles. Diagnosis is mainly clinical, supported by otoscopy and, where available, pneumatic otoscopy or tympanometry.
b: Otoscopy: look for bulging, retraction or perforation

t.b: Assesses tympanic membrane mobility; reduced mobility suggests effusion or otitis media
Measures middle‑ear pressure; type B indicates fluid, type C negative pressure

sections.p: Acute otitis media (AOM) is staged by symptom duration and severity. Chronic otitis media with effusion (COME) is defined by fluid lasting >3 months. Complications such as mastoiditis are graded by extent of bone erosion and spread.

t.b: Detects hearing loss; a 20‑dB shift indicates significant conductive loss

sections.p: In East Africa, the leading causes are viral upper respiratory infections, bacterial superinfection (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae), and allergic rhinitis. Malnutrition and HIV increase susceptibility.
b: Bacterial superinfection → pus in middle ear

t.b: Rules out viral cause; positive suggests supportive care

sections.p: Children with middle‑ear disease may be irritable, tug at ears, have fever, or show poor feeding. Otoscopic findings include bulging, erythema, or perforation. Hearing loss may be subtle.

t.b: Identifies conductive hearing loss; a 15‑dB shift is clinically relevant

sections.p: Investigations are limited in low‑resource settings. Basic otoscopy is essential; tympanometry and audiometry are ideal but often unavailable. When possible, cultures of middle‑ear fluid guide antibiotic choice.

t.b: Identifies causative organism; guides antibiotic selection

sections.p: Urgent red flags include severe pain, fever >39°C, bulging tympanic membrane with haemorrhage, facial weakness, or signs of mastoiditis. Complications can be life‑threatening, such as meningitis or brain abscess.

t.b: Detects mastoid bone erosion or intracranial spread

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause: antibiotics for bacterial AOM, supportive care for viral. Use analgesia, keep the child hydrated, and advise parents on ear protection. Avoid steroids unless indicated for severe inflammation.

t.b: First‑line for AOM; chosen for efficacy and low resistance in many settings
Reduces pain and fever; preferred over NSAIDs in children

sections.p: Re‑evaluate in 48‑72 hours; if symptoms persist, consider referral. Prevention focuses on vaccination (PCV, Hib), hand hygiene, and avoiding smoke exposure.

t.b: Ensures protection against common bacterial pathogens

sections.p: Otitis externa, acute mastoiditis, and cholesteatoma can mimic middle‑ear disease. Otitis externa presents with ear canal pain and discharge, while mastoiditis shows swelling behind the ear.
Pneumatic otoscopy may appear normal in early effusion; tympanometry type B can be seen in both AOM and COME. In malnutrition, hearing tests may underestimate loss.

t.b: Type B may not distinguish AOM from COME without clinical context

whenToSeekHelp: Severe ear pain unrelieved by analgesia

faq.q: What is the most common bacterial cause of AOM in children?
faq.a: Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae are the leading bacteria.

faq.q: When should I refer for a CT scan?
faq.a: If there is mastoid swelling, facial nerve palsy, or no improvement after 48‑72 hours of antibiotics.

faq.q: Can I use ibuprofen for ear pain?
faq.a: Yes, but avoid if the child has bleeding disorders or is on anticoagulants.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order for a child with suspected AOM in a low‑resource setting? — Otoscopy; if unavailable, a rapid viral test to rule out influenza.
How would you differentiate otitis media from otitis externa on examination? — Otitis externa shows canal pain and discharge; otitis media shows bulging TM and no canal discharge.

A child presents with fever, ear tugging and a bulging tympanic membrane. What antibiotic would you start and why? — Amoxicillin; first‑line, effective against S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae, low resistance in many settings.
What red flag would prompt immediate referral for possible mastoiditis? — Swelling behind the ear or facial nerve weakness.
If tympanometry shows a type B curve but the child is asymptomatic, what is the likely diagnosis? — Chronic otitis media with effusion; asymptomatic but fluid present.
A child with AOM is not improving after 48 hours of antibiotics. What is the next step? — Re‑evaluate, consider culture‑guided therapy, and assess for complications.
Why is a rapid antigen test for influenza useful in this context? — It helps distinguish viral from bacterial causes, guiding supportive versus antibiotic treatment.
